segments.text: Good afternoon. Before anything else, can I check your full name and date of birth for me?
Oh, yes. It's Winifred Pemberton. Fourteenth of March, nineteen forty-nine. Is that... have I said it right?
Perfect, thank you, Mrs. Pemberton. I can see you're here for a review of your bones. What would you like to talk about?
Well, it was my daughter who made the appointment, really. She said I ought to come, because of my back, and, um...
Take your time. What's your back been doing?
It aches. Down low, on the right side. Not all the time, but when I bend over to do the garden it's quite... well, it catches me.
Okay. When did the backache begin, roughly?
Oh dear. That's the thing. I couldn't tell you. It might have been around Christmas, or perhaps before that, in the autumn? I really can't say.
That's fine, an approximate idea is all I need. Was there a particular moment, like lifting something or a fall?
No, no. I can't think of one. It just sort of... crept up.
Have you had any falls at all in the last year?
No, none. I'm very careful, I hold on to the banister, and I've got those mats with the grips in the bathroom.
Good. Now I understand you were told your bones were thin on a scan, is that correct?
Yes, osteoporosis, that's what they called it. The doctor before you said I should have been on something for it by now, but I never... I wasn't happy with it.
Mm. Can you tell me why you weren't happy with it?
I think I had a reaction. I'm fairly sure I'm allergic to one of the bone tablets, I took it once for a short while. But I couldn't tell you which one, or what happened exactly.
That matters a lot, so let's slow down. You think you're allergic to one of the bone tablets, but you can't recall the name, and you don't remember the reaction?
That's right. I remember feeling poorly. And my sister said I was ever so upset about it. But whether it was a rash, or my tummy, or... I'm sorry.
No need to apologise. Roughly how long ago was that?
Ten years? Perhaps fifteen. It was a long time back.
And is there anyone who might remember more, or any papers at home, like a hospital letter or a pharmacy bag?
My sister might. Marjorie. She keeps everything. I could ask her to look.
Please do. I'd rather we knew what it was before we choose a treatment. Have you had any other reactions to medicines that you can remember?
No, not that I... no. It's just that one.
Okay, then. Mrs. Pemberton, may I have a feel of your back? Would you stand and bend forwards a little for me?
Of course. Do I need to take my cardigan off?
Just lift it at the back, please. Tell me if I press somewhere that hurts.
Oh! There. Yes, just there, that's the spot.
Yes, there's one spot of tenderness over the lower spine on the right. Everything else moves nicely. You can sit back down.
Is it serious, doctor? I've been so worried it's something I've done.
You haven't done anything. Here's where I am. The ache could simply be a strained muscle. But with thin bones, I can't rule out a small crack in one of the vertebrae.
A crack? In my spine?
A small compression fracture can happen in osteoporosis, sometimes with very little force, and it can creep up just like you described.
Oh, goodness. I don't like the sound of that at all.
I know. It's not certain, and I don't want to alarm you. Whatever it turns out to be, there are ways to protect your bones.
What sort of ways?

Let me list the broad options, no names for now. A tablet taken weekly, a drip once a year, or an injection every six months. Which suits depends on your kidneys, your stomach, and importantly, that possible allergy.
I think I'd prefer the one that's the least bother. My stomach doesn't like tablets much.
That's helpful to know. In the meantime, gentle walking is good for bone, and foods with calcium, like yoghurt, cheese and green leafy vegetables. Keep using the grip mats and the banister.
I do like cheese. My daughter says I eat too much of it.
For once, I'd side with your cheese habit. Please also bend from your knees, not your back, when you're in the garden.
I'll try. The weeds don't pull themselves, though.
They'll wait. Next, can I ask you to find out from your sister what that tablet was, or whatever she remembers about it?
Yes, I'll ring her tonight. She goes to bed late.
Good. Then I'd like to see you again in six weeks, once we know more, and we'll choose a treatment together.
Six weeks. Right. I'll put it on the fridge calendar so I don't forget.
Lovely. And if the back pain suddenly gets much worse, call the surgery the same day.
I will. Thank you for explaining it all, doctor. Nobody has before.
You're very welcome. Mind the step on the way out.
